items.content:
RT @GrapheneOS: We have a partial port of GrapheneOS to the Pixel 11 series after a week of work on it. We're unable to complete the port due to lack of support for ARM hardware memory tagging in software, firmware and near certainly hardware. It appears Google cut an important security feature to save money.

ARM hardware memory tagging (MTE) is used by GrapheneOS across the entire base OS including the kernel and every standard base OS process. It's only temporarily disabled for a few device-specific processes. It greatly improves protection against nearly all remote exploits and many local exploits.

Pixel 8 launched with hardware MTE support in October 2023. We integrated it into our hardened_malloc project and began using it across the OS later that month. Android and the Pixel OS never started using it by default. Android Advanced Protection Mode in Android 16 enables it for a few processes.

Apple's Memory Integrity Enforcement (MIE) is an always enabled feature on the iPhone 17. It's simply a high quality implementation of MTE using the latest standard extensions. It uses MTE in the most secure mode in the kernel and a large portion of userbase. They did a very good job integrating it.

Apple's MIE and Android 16+ AAPM don't use MTE for user installed apps unless those explicitly opt in. GrapheneOS enables it for more apps automatically and has a toggle for users to opt-in for every user installed app. There's a per-app toggle to opt-out for incompatible apps which is uncommon.

Neither iOS or Android encourage app developers to opt into MTE and other more aggressive security features used in the base OS. Apple's docs warn developers of performance and stability issues. Even Signal doesn't opt-in. Our approach enables forcing using MTE in the standard allocators regardless.

Pixel 11 does have security improvements including moving to post-quantum secure verified boot (ML-DSA) and replacing Samsung Shannon IMS with AOSP IMS. Titan M3 should significantly improve protection against data extraction in Before First Unlock state. It's too bad they ruined it by cutting MTE.

Pixel 11 series is a lot more expensive for an incremental improvement to the CPU, the same underpowered GPU and reduced RAM for the Pro base models. They finally caught up to the last generation of Qualcomm cellular radio. It's overpriced, the upgrades aren't impressive and losing MTE is appalling.

Compared to the Pixel 11, a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 has ~40% higher single threaded CPU performance, ~80% higher multi threaded performance, over 100% higher GPU performance and a far better cellular radio. It also finally has MTE. The next gen is what will be in the first Motorola with GrapheneOS.

Pixel 9a and earlier (including Nexus devices) were the Android Open Source Project reference devices. Pixel support was removed from AOSP with Android 16. It's now harder to support Pixels than many other devices and massive progress towards open source firmware and driver libraries was discarded.

Compared to the stock Pixel OS, GrapheneOS ships AOSP patches months earlier and Linux kernel patches many months earlier. However, we rely on them for firmware and most driver updates. We also want to move to new kernel branches earlier. These things can be improved with our Motorola partnership.

We strongly recommend against buying Pixel 11 devices. Pixel 8, 9 and 10 have much better overall security for GrapheneOS. Pixel 10 is cheaper with similar hardware and MTE. Pixel 11's Titan M3 should improve BFU security for users without a strong passphrase, but losing MTE craters AFU security.

We haven't determined what to do about this situation. It may be best for us to skip the Pixel 11 series devices. We can shift our focus entirely to the upcoming Motorola devices instead. Pixel 10a was really a 9th gen Pixel, so hopefully the Pixel 11a does the same with 10th gen and includes MTE.

RT @lukhash: I'll soon be sharing my live #chiptune instrument for the C64/C64U - SID SYNTH 👾 It sits between two amazing programs, the instant playability of Cynthcart and the deep sound design of SID Wizard. That's the middle ground I've been missing. The ultimate tool for live performance on your favourite computer :)

For those who are interested what's under the hood:

Eight waveforms (4 main+combined ones) across three voices (six with a second SID), an adjustable ADSR with hard-restart retrigger, a multimode filter, and fully customisable PWM with its own rate, depth and sweep shapes. Add vibrato, portamento and tremolo, plus switchable ring mod and hard sync. Seven voice modes take you from full polyphony through fifths and octave stacks to arpeggios you can lock to tempo. Then you play it: live pitch bend, vibrato swells and filter swipes you can freeze and latch mid-note, for real expression and sound design beyond presets.

Build your own banks of instruments across 54 slots, save and load them to disk, and jump between sounds on the fly, so a whole set is under your fingers on stage, with a "Live Lock" to keep a stray key from changing anything mid-song.

Full MIDI in adds assignable CC to use with your DAW or any MIDI hardware, program change to switch patches hands-free, and clock sync to keep the arpeggiator in time with your drum machine or sequencer, plus a tap-tempo that sets the arpeggiator's speed straight from the rhythm you tap, so you can lock the arp to your track by ear in seconds.

Twelve reactive visualizers turn a held note into a show, and dual-SID stereo, blackout-clean recording for the real SID chip and automatic PAL/NTSC tuning finish the picture.

We just released OrcaRouter’s uncensored weights for GLM-5.3-Flash — 320B parameters / 18B active, directly at the original block-FP8 precision.

No LoRA. No jailbreak prompt. Refusal removal is baked directly into the weights.

The evals are particularly interesting:

→ MaliciousInstruct refusal: 96% → 11%
→ JailbreakBench: 93% → 12%
→ AdvBench: 97% → 15%
→ HarmBench: 93% → 18%

That makes this release interesting beyond uncensoring: it's a useful artifact for studying how frontier-model alignment is actually represented inside the network.

items.content:
We had an Ubuntu web server that suddenly started making outbound HTTPS connections late at night.

Nothing was down.

The website was still working normally.

CPU and memory looked fine, so at first there was nothing serious to suggest the server had been compromised.

I logged in and started checking the running services.

One service caught my attention:

system-update.service

The name looked normal enough. On a Linux server, you can easily assume something like that belongs to the operating system.

I checked the actual service file.

Its ExecStart was pointing to:

/usr/local/bin/.system-update

That was where things stopped looking normal.

It was a hidden executable inside /usr/local/bin, running as a systemd service and configured with:

Restart=always

Meaning if the process died, systemd would simply start it again.

I checked the file.

It was a stripped 64-bit ELF binary.

Then I pulled the PID for the service and checked its network connections.

The process had an established connection to an external IP over port 443.

So now we had a suspicious binary, persistence through systemd and an active outbound connection.

The next question was how it got there.

I checked the timestamps.

The service had been created around 6:43 PM the previous evening.

Then I went through the authentication logs.

This was the part that really caught my attention.

A few seconds before the service was created, the www-data account had executed commands with sudo.

www-data is normally the account used by the web server.

It should not casually be copying executables into /usr/local/bin and enabling system services as root.

The logs showed it copying the hidden binary from /tmp, reloading systemd and enabling the new service.

At that point we isolated the server.

We did not immediately conclude exactly how the attacker got control of www-data, because the evidence we had did not prove the initial entry point yet.

It could have been the web application, a vulnerable plugin, bad sudo permissions or something else entirely.

That became the next part of the investigation.

But one thing was already clear:

system-update.service was not a Linux update service.

Someone had simply given it a boring name and hoped nobody would check what it actually executed.

And to be fair, if we had only looked at the service name, we probably would have passed it.

That is why when I see an unfamiliar Linux service now, I don’t stop at systemctl status.

I want to see the unit file.

I want to see the executable.

I want to know who created it and what that process is talking to.

Names can lie.

The path usually tells you more.

RT @DailyDarkWeb: 🇷🇺🚨 LEAK EXPOSES RUSSIA'S PIPELINE FOR TRAINING FUTURE MILITARY CYBER OPERATORS

A newly analyzed leak from Bauman Moscow State Technical University provides a rare look inside what researchers assess to be a long-term training pipeline feeding personnel into Russia's military intelligence and cyber operations apparatus.

DomainTools Investigations analyzed approximately 1,600 leaked files from Bauman University's secretive Department No. 4, including personnel records, curricula, examinations, internship records, presentations, correspondence and planning documents.

The findings are significant:

* Roughly 250 career and reserve students were trained across three military specialties
* Training covered offensive cyber operations, defensive security, technical intelligence and information operations
* Coursework included password attacks, server exploitation, software vulnerabilities, malware creation, penetration testing, cryptography, intrusion detection and technical surveillance
* Students participated in attacker-vs-defender exercises and cyber-range-style training
* Internship records show placements at Russian military units and academies
* Reported graduates were assigned to GRU Military Unit 26165 — associated with APT28 / Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard
* Other graduates were reportedly assigned to GRU Military Unit 74455 — associated with Sandworm / APT44
* Senior GRU officers were reportedly involved in student evaluation and oversight
* The largest training stream focused on operational "information-technical effects" — effectively integrating offensive and defensive cyber capabilities into military operations

The leaked archive was distributed through DarkForums, where a newly created account named "Losyash" posted links to approximately 1.8 GB of data.

DomainTools says metadata analysis of the files, internal structures, personnel records and subsequent journalistic corroboration support its assessment that the material originated from Bauman University.

However, exactly how the files were initially obtained remains unknown.

⚠️ Analyst Note:

The most interesting finding isn't simply that Russia trains hackers.

The documents appear to expose an institutionalized cyber force-generation pipeline: recruitment → technical education → adversary simulation → military placement → operational units.

This suggests Russia's cyber capability should not be viewed solely through individual APT groups such as APT28 or Sandworm.

Behind those operational units appears to be a repeatable system designed to continuously produce cyber operators, intelligence specialists, planners, defenders and reserve personnel.

The leak potentially provides researchers with an unusually detailed opportunity to map the human infrastructure behind future Russian military cyber operations.

Source: DomainTools Investigations — August 26, 2026
https://t.co/sh7EPQfhLr

#DDW #ThreatIntelligence #GRU #APT28 #Sandworm

items.content:
RT @Byron_Wan: 🚨 UK security officials fear the sprawling 15-acre City of Dreams Mediterranean complex in Cyprus could have harboured visitors with a deeper agenda than topping up their tans and eating in the various gourmet restaurants.

The Chinese-owned hotel — a stone’s throw from the border of Britain’s military complex in Cyprus — allows guests a bird’s-eye view over one of the UK’s most critical overseas bases.

Several intelligence and military sources said that they feared foreign spies could have used the City of Dreams as an observation post.

The luxury resort, which opened in 2023, dominates the landscape: taller than any surrounding building by quite some distance.

Unlike many of Limassol’s high-end hotels, however, it does not boast a beachfront location, but borders the UK sovereign base area. The territory is home to RAF Akrotiri — the nexus of Britain’s strategic operations in the Middle East and a crucial staging post for the US war against Iran.

The hotel’s proximity, bordering UK sovereign territory on two sides, has drawn the attention of senior military figures within Akrotiri, as well as security officials. They believe the towering City of Dreams resort offers prime surveillance opportunities.

With nothing more than a pair of binoculars and the right vantage point, an observer could spot planes taking off and landing, as well as officials and troops moving in and around the base.

Shaped like a pyramid, the hotel’s suites stack one on top of the other, forming a wide base that narrows as it ascends before flattening out at the top.

Access to the top floor, and its prime viewing platform, is restricted unless you are renting one of the two “presidential suites”.

The imposing size of the white stone and glass structure starkly contrasts with its neighbouring buildings.

Outside, cream canvas sun loungers and parasols face lagoon-style pools that look out towards the British sovereign base area, along with a dozen tennis courts.

Inside, the hotel features Europe’s first integrated casino, lit up by a giant chandelier and flashing, multi-coloured slot machines. All four of the resort’s restaurants are accessed from this central area.

The hotel is part of a chain held by Melco Resorts, led by the Chinese-Canadian billionaire Lawrence Ho.

The businessman sits on 🇨🇳 National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), described as a “patriotic united front” organization.

Figures within RAF Akrotiri have voiced concerns that the hotel could be used as an espionage base by Chinese authorities.

There is no suggestion of any wrongdoing by Ho, or his company’s hotel.

The top floor of the 16-storey hotel could offer the perfect lookout over a busy military base.

Akrotiri is particularly sensitive because it houses the F-35, the world’s most advanced stealth fighter jet, and the U-2 Dragon Lady, the US spy plane.

During the early phase of the Iran war, a drone linked to Tehran struck the U-2 operations at Akrotiri as part of its region-wide reaction to attacks by the US and Israel.

To carry out such an accurate strike, the Islamic Republic would probably have collected intelligence from allies.

With the City of Dreams Mediterranean hotel on its radar, RAF Akrotiri would be deploying counter-surveillance measures. But there are limits to what can be done to foil espionage operations, and they expressed concerns about the base’s security.

City of Dreams’s proximity could give Beijing an observation post overlooking the base at Akrotiri. From there, spies could collect a multitude of basic data, such as patterns of movement, operational procedures, sortie rates, information on perimeter security and patrols, counter-drone responses or visual confirmation of flights not publicly broadcasting their details.

Having “eyes on” is considered an “advantage”.

items.content:
RT @Itsfoss: Debian has now officially voted to allow the use of generative AI in project contributions.

After days/weeks of discussion and voting, here's what Debian has decided.

AI tools are permitted for development, maintenance, and documentation work. They can improve contributor productivity when used responsibly.

But every AI-assisted contribution must meet the same quality, correctness, and legal standards as any other. No exemptions.

Contributors must understand, review, test, and where needed, modify AI-generated output before submitting it. The responsibility stays entirely with the human.

Disclosure of AI use is encouraged but not mandatory.

Sharing confidential or security-sensitive information with third-party AI services is explicitly not allowed.

Large-scale automated changes need prior community discussion and human oversight before going through.

............

Debian is doing the balancing act. Outright ban on AI may lead to dwindling contributors as developers increasingly rely on AI assistance. But letting AI lose will turn into slopfest. 

Your thoughts?

items.content:
RT @Officialwhyte22: The owner had already changed the battery once.

A few days later, the same thing happened again.

The car would sit overnight and by morning the battery was weak enough that starting it became a problem. At first, everything pointed toward the usual suspects: alternator, interior lights, an accessory staying powered, or maybe just another bad battery.

But when I started looking at the vehicle network, something else stood out.

The ignition was off, the doors were closed, and the car had been sitting long enough that most of the control modules should have started going to sleep.

The CAN bus was still busy.

That caught my attention.

Modern cars do not shut everything down immediately after you turn the ignition off. Some modules stay awake for a while to save data, monitor the alarm system, manage locks, communicate with other ECUs, and finish background tasks.

But after a certain period, most of that activity should reduce significantly.

So I connected to the CAN interface and watched the traffic.

At first, there were plenty of frames moving across the bus, which was normal.

Then the traffic slowly started dropping as different modules went quiet.

Except for one group of CAN IDs.

They kept appearing.

Minute after minute.

I checked the bus activity again and it was still higher than I expected for a vehicle that should have been settling into its sleep state.

That gave me something real to investigate.

One module, or something connected to it, appeared to be keeping part of the network awake.

And when one ECU refuses to sleep, it can sometimes keep other modules awake with it. That means several electronic systems can continue drawing power for hours while the car is parked.

From the owner’s perspective, it looks like a battery problem.

From the network side, it looks completely different.

Now, this does not automatically mean anything malicious is happening.

A bad body control module, faulty door sensor, infotainment system, telematics unit, wiring issue, software bug, or another ECU can all cause similar behaviour.

But instead of replacing another battery and hoping for the best, the CAN traffic gives you somewhere to start.

Which module is still transmitting?

When should it normally stop?

Is something waking the network back up?

Does the same CAN ID remain active every time the vehicle is switched off?

This is one reason I find automobile cybersecurity auditing so interesting.

Sometimes the problem people see as purely mechanical or electrical is actually sitting quietly inside the communication between the computers running the car.
